The worker became a police officer in 1986. In 1992, he was seconded into a joint forces special project. In December 1992, he was interviewed by officers from the internal investigations bureau. The worker's name had come up in the course of a wiretap investigation of an individual, D, who was accused of conspiracy to commit murder. The worker had a personal and business relationship with D going back to 1989. The worker was then assigned to desk duty. The employer conducted an investigation into the worker's connections with D. The worker stopped working in January 1993 due to stress-related disability. In the spring of 1993, the worker was charged under the Police Services Act with insubordination, neglect of duty and discreditable conduct. In April 1994, he was found not guilty on all counts. In May 1994, his emotional condition resolved and he returned to work. The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Officer denying entitlement for stress-related disability.

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 1897/98 was denied. The original decision was based on a settlement proposed by the worker's representative and agreed to by the original vice-chair. The worker submitted that he did not understand the agreement on which the decision was based. The Vice-Chair stated that compelling evidence would be required to set aside a final decision of the Tribunal on the basis of an alleged misunderstanding. In this case, there was no substantive evidence of a misunderstanding. The onus of proof is on the party seeking reconsideration to demonstrate that there was a fundamental error in the original process. The worker did not meet that evidentiary burden.

DecSummary: The worker and her husband operated a cleaning company. The worker was injured in July 1994. She had personal coverage in the amount of $50,000. The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 125/98 was denied. The delay of 17 years before requesting the reconsideration made unreasonable to re-open or clarify the decision.
